name: LTC6902CMS#TRPBF
title: LTC6902: resistor-set multiphase oscillator, 2, 3 or 4 phases, with spread spectrum frequency modulation, 5 kHz to 20 MHz, MSOP-10
summary: A clock oscillator whose frequency is fixed by one resistor from V+ to SET and whose four CMOS outputs give two, three or four phases of the same clock. A master oscillator running from 100 kHz to 20 MHz feeds a divider of 1, 10 or 100 chosen by the three-level DIV pin, then a phase circuit chosen by the three-level PH pin, so the output covers 5 kHz to 20 MHz. A second resistor, from V+ to MOD, adds pseudorandom downward frequency modulation to spread the clock's energy; grounding MOD turns it off. It runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V and comes in a 10-lead MSOP, as the LTC6902C and the LTC6902I.

pins.name: V+
pins.function: Supply, 2.7 V to 5.5 V. Keep it free of noise and ripple; decouple with 0.1 µF to a ground plane, right at the pin.

pins.name: DIV
pins.function: Selects N, the divide ratio after the master oscillator: GND gives ÷1 (highest range), open gives ÷10, V+ gives ÷100 (lowest range). The pin sits at mid-supply when open, so pulling it to either rail takes about 2 µA. When left open, decouple it with 1 nF to GND or surround it with a ground guard against coupling from nearby traces.

pins.name: PH
pins.function: Selects the phase mode and M: GND gives 2-phase (M = 1, highest range), open gives 3-phase (M = 3), V+ gives 4-phase (M = 4, lowest range). The pin sits at mid-supply when open, so pulling it to either rail takes about 2 µA. When left open, decouple it with 1 nF to GND or surround it with a ground guard.

pins.name: OUT1
pins.function: Clock output, phase 1. Drives 5 kΩ and/or 10 pF; heavier loads can cost accuracy through supply bounce at high frequency.

pins.name: OUT2
pins.function: Clock output, phase 2. Same load rating as OUT1.

pins.name: OUT3
pins.function: Clock output, phase 3. Same load rating as OUT1.

pins.name: OUT4
pins.function: Clock output, phase 4; held low in 3-phase mode. Same load rating as OUT1.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground; tie to a ground plane.

pins.name: MOD
pins.function: Spreading resistor RMOD, from this pin to V+, sets the depth of frequency modulation, always downward from the RSET frequency. Tie to GND to disable modulation and power down its circuits; an open pin also gives 0 % in theory but picks up noise that disturbs accuracy. RMOD should be a precision metal-film part between 10k and 2M, with under 10 pF on the pin; its voltage moves.

pins.name: SET
pins.function: Frequency-setting resistor RSET goes from this pin to V+. The pin is held about 1.13 V below V+. RSET should be a precision metal-film part between 10k and 2M, and keep the pin's capacitance under 10 pF.

circuits.title: 500kHz, 4-phase clock with 20% frequency spreading
circuits.description: The oscillator on a 5 V supply giving four 500 kHz clocks a quarter period apart. PH tied to V+ picks 4-phase mode (M = 4); DIV left open picks ÷10; RSET = 10k sets fOUT = 10 MHz/(10 × 4) × 20k/10k = 500 kHz. RMOD = 10k, equal to RSET, gives 20 × 10k/10k = 20 % downward spreading. The 0.1 µF capacitor decouples V+.
notes: DIV is open (N = 10).

circuits.title: Typical application with design equation
circuits.description: The general hookup that the design equations describe: RSET from V+ to SET sets the frequency, RMOD from V+ to MOD sets the spreading, DIV and PH are each tied to GND, left open or tied to V+ to pick N and M, and 0.1 µF decouples V+. fOUT = 10 MHz/(N × M) × 20 kΩ/RSET for 5 kHz ≤ fOUT ≤ 20 MHz; spreading = 20 × RSET/RMOD percent.
notes: For a fixed frequency RMOD is left out and MOD goes to GND.

operation.text: The master oscillator's frequency follows the current into it divided by the voltage across RSET (V+ – VSET). A PMOS stage holds SET about 1.1 V under V+ (±8 % at a given current and supply; it falls as IRES rises). Because RSET ties that voltage to ISET, accuracy does not depend on the exact SET voltage. RSET of 10k to 2M gives a master frequency of 100 kHz to 20 MHz; accuracy can suffer above 10 MHz with a supply under 4 V.

The master output is divided by 1, 10 or 100 (DIV at GND or below 0.5 V, open or mid-supply, at V+ or within 0.4 V of it), then by the phase circuit, which divides further by M = 1, 3 or 4 and drives the four output buffers. The overlapping divider ranges mean frequencies near 100 kHz and 1 MHz can be reached with two RSET values.

The CMOS outputs have an on-resistance typically under 100 Ω and behave much like HCMOS logic outputs. In ÷1 mode edges are typically 7 ns at 5 V and 11 ns at 3 V, enough for a clean 10 MHz square wave (20 MHz at 5 V). In ÷10 and ÷100 a slew-rate limit stretches edges to typically 14 ns at 5 V and 19 ns at 3 V, lowering EMI and supply bounce.

With SSFM on, a modulation current IMOD is taken from ISET, so the master frequency only ever drops below the RSET value (downspread). V+ – VMOD comes from a multiplying DAC referenced to VSET: it is one fifth of (V+ – VSET) times the DAC code, between 0 V and 20 % of V+ – VSET. With RSET = RMOD, IMOD swings 0 to 0.2 ISET and the frequency between fMAX and 0.8 fMAX. The code comes from a 9-bit linear feedback shift register (sequence of 512); its low seven bits drive the DAC, giving 128 steps. The register is clocked by the master oscillator divided by 3200, and a servo loop of about 25 kHz bandwidth smooths the steps.
Tie MOD to GND: this stops modulation and shuts down the modulation circuitry. Leaving MOD open gives 0 % in theory, but the open pin picks up noise that disturbs the output frequency.

The master covers 200:1 and the divider steps 10:1, so most frequencies have at least two solutions. For SSFM, use the highest divider so the master, which clocks the pseudorandom generator, runs fastest; faster modulation gives more EMC improvement. For fixed frequency, the highest divider gives the lowest jitter (division reduces master jitter), while the lowest divider gives the best accuracy and lowest power because the master runs slower. M can also be used to move the master up or down: a single clock can take whichever mode gives the wanted M, and two phases can come from OUT1 and OUT3 (or OUT2 and OUT4) in 4-phase mode.
4-phase, 250 kHz clock with 40 % spreading: PH to V+ (M = 4), DIV open (N = 10), RSET = 20k sets fOUT = fMAX = 250 kHz, RMOD = 10k sets 40 % spreading.

The part is aimed at clocking several interleaved switching regulators at one frequency, which reduces input capacitance and avoids beat notes. Because the phases come through inverters or flip-flops, rising (or falling) edges of different outputs never coincide, even with heavy spreading. Most regulators synchronize on the clock's rising edge. The 25 kHz smoothing keeps each frequency change within a regulator's loop bandwidth (typically 1/10, ranging 1/50 to 1/2 of its switching frequency); a regulator with bandwidth above 25 kHz stays in regulation. A PLL-synchronized regulator needs a loop filter with enough capture range and bandwidth. Output ripple becomes noise-like and broadband instead of a repeating tone, and the sequence repeats well below the audio band.

The outputs can drive general digital logic, but the pseudorandom modulation, though smoothed by the 25 kHz filter, gives more cycle-to-cycle jitter than a slow triangular modulation, so logic with tight timing needs that jitter checked.

For best EMC run SSFM with the master at its highest frequency. Modulating at or above the measuring bandwidth of regulatory tests gives the lowest readings; for interference inside a system the best rate has to be found in that system, within the regulator's synchronization range.
The guaranteed voltage coefficient is 0.1 %/V; typical sensitivity is half that.

Keep the capacitance on SET and on MOD under 10 pF; more capacitance on SET raises jitter. Decouple V+ with 0.1 µF right at the pin to a ground plane, tie GND to the plane, and give an open DIV or PH pin 1 nF to GND or a ground guard.
